summary:
TerraWaltz reads radar time-series the way musicians read rhythm. NISAR and Sentinel-1 watch wetlands, farms, and glaciers through cloud and darkness, but raw backscatter is unreadable to most people — so we taught each pixel a "Dance
  DNA": its tempo, amplitude, and coherence over time, distilled into a 0–100 Rhythm Break Score that flags when a place stops behaving like itself.

  We built an open-source web platform with four sites trained on real Sentinel-1 data (Louisiana, Assam in India, Fraser in BC, and the Mekong), a real NISAR L-band granule rendered in-app, flood-event modeling from three monsoon seasons, a
  layer showing water L-band sees that C-band misses, 12-day NISAR change analysis, and impact reports quantifying people and cropland in harm's way. It turns complex radar into ranked alerts, plain-English explanations, and sound — because
  when a wetland stops dancing, someone should hear it before the land is gone.
details:
TerraWaltz is an open-source interactive platform that translates NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar observations into dance. Earth's surface is constantly moving — wetlands breathe with the seasons, rice paddies pulse with planting cycles,

  glaciers surge and calve — but raw synthetic aperture radar (SAR) backscatter is nearly unreadable outside the remote-sensing community. Our core idea is that every pixel has a rhythm, and that change matters most when the rhythm breaks.

  What it does and how it works. For every map cell we compute a "Dance DNA" fingerprint from its multi-year VV/VH backscatter time-series: tempo (dominant seasonal period), amplitude, coherence stability, trend, and phase lag. A

  RandomForest trained per site on Sentinel-1 RTC scenes (2019–2026) with JRC Global Surface Water labels classifies water and wetland behavior using spatial-block hold-out validation, train-only threshold calibration, and tree-disagreement

  confidence maps. The Rhythm Break Score (0–100) combines harmonic residual, coherence drop, polarization shift, and trend break to rank anomalies: Louisiana (F1 0.993), Assam, India (0.974), Fraser River Delta, Canada (0.957), and the

  Mekong (0.800 after retraining). A dedicated flood-event model for Assam was trained on change-detection reference extents from the July 2020, 2022, and 2024 monsoon floods (F1 0.950). We downloaded a real NISAR L2 GCOV granule from ASF

  (7.3 GB, 100% coverage of Assam) and differenced two 12-day repeat passes to produce genuine NISAR-versus-NISAR change. A "Duet" layer shows where L-band sees water under canopy that C-band misses (10.6% of Assam cells). The app layers

  these with pre-rendered cloud-optimized tiles, a guided cinematic tour, next-step forecast cones, cross-site "rhythm twin" search, real WorldPop/ESA WorldCover exposure estimates, and operator-gated webhook/SMS alert dispatch with audit

  logging.

  Tools and technology. JavaScript (Node.js, zero-dependency server and serverless API), HTML/CSS canvas rendering, Python (rasterio, scikit-learn, Planetary Computer STAC and ASF APIs), data from NASA Earthdata/ASF (NISAR, Sentinel-1), JRC

  Global Surface Water, WorldPop, and ESA WorldCover, developed locally on a laptop GPU-free and deployed for Vercel.

  Creativity and factors considered. Rather than another before/after change map, TerraWaltz classifies temporal behavior — Waltz (seasonal), Tango (abrupt), Drift (subsidence), Broken (anomalous) — adds sonification so a missed flood can be

  heard, and publishes its weak scores (Mekong's original F1 0.466 and a negative L-band ablation) as openly as its strong ones. We prioritized honesty (spatial hold-outs, proxy labels flagged, pilot-not-operational warnings), accessibility

  (plain-English explanations, English/Spanish), and reproducibility (MIT license, full test suite).

  Benefits and intended impact. Flood officers, coastal managers, and farmers get ranked, plain-language alerts with population exposure attached — "inspect these cells this week" instead of a GeoTIFF weeks later. We hope TerraWaltz becomes

  trusted early-warning infrastructure for delta communities facing intensifying floods and land loss, and a teaching tool that lets anyone dance with the SARs.

1. Rhythm, not snapshots. Others map before/after change; we fingerprint each pixel's temporal behavior (Dance DNA) and score when it breaks character — a normal flood scores low, a missing flood scores 87.

  2. The Duet layer. First app to show, from real granules, where NISAR L-band sees water under canopy that Sentinel-1 C-band cannot (10.6% of Assam) — flooded forest invisible to every C-band-only project.

  3. Real NISAR time, not logos. A downloaded 7.3 GB GCOV granule rendered in-app, plus two 12-day repeat passes differenced into genuine NISAR-vs-NISAR change.

  4. Forecast + twins. A next-step prediction cone per pixel, and cross-continent rhythm-twin search (find pixels in other sites dancing the same shape).

  5. Honesty as a feature. Confidence heatmaps everywhere, weak scores (Mekong 0.47→0.80) and a failed L-band ablation published, pilot-not-operational stamped on every alert.

  6. You can hear it. Sonification turns backscatter into pitch and coherence loss into dissonance — a missed flood is a note that never comes.
